questions.question: What is a database index and why is it important?
questions.title: Database Indexes — What They Are and Why They Matter
questions.direct_answer: A database index is an auxiliary access structure that helps the optimizer locate or order rows without scanning/sorting the whole table in suitable queries. B-tree is common, but hash, bitmap-style, full-text, spatial, and other index types exist. An index can make reads faster, but not every query uses it, and it costs storage, cache, write work, and maintenance.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand an index trades faster reads for slower writes/space.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Indexing everything, assuming indexes are free.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention B-tree structure, O(log n) lookups, and write/storage overhead.

sections.title: What a Database Index Does
sections.content:
Unique constraints are often enforced through an index, but a performance index and a logical constraint are different design purposes. Covering indexes can satisfy a query from index entries, while partial/filtered indexes store only qualifying rows in supported databases.

Use EXPLAIN/ANALYZE and production-like data. Keep statistics current and measure writes as well as reads before adding or removing an index.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Indexes store keys plus row locators or clustered-key information.
They can support filters, joins, ordering, uniqueness, or covering reads.
Selectivity, leading columns, expressions, collation, and query shape decide usefulness.
Use the optimizer plan and workload metrics rather than assuming an index always helps.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: An index on orders(customer_id, created_at) can efficiently find one customer's recent orders and may avoid an extra sort. A query returning most orders may use a table scan because reading the index and then many rows costs more. Each insert also updates the index, so unused/duplicate indexes reduce write capacity. The book-index analogy explains lookup, but database indexes are not all simply sorted copies of one column.

sections.title: Indexes at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~sorted structure|usually a B-tree|maps value -> row|like a book index
emerald|Speeds up|~reads|WHERE lookups|JOIN matching|ORDER BY sorting
rose|Costs|~not free|slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE|extra storage|index maintenance
amber|Lookup|~O(log n)|vs O(n) full scan|huge on big tables|

sections.title: Create an index and see it help
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Indexing everything**: each index slows writes and uses space — index columns you actually filter/join on.
- **Indexing low-cardinality columns**: an index on a boolean rarely helps.
- **Function on the column**: `WHERE LOWER(email) = ...` skips a plain index.
- **Forgetting maintenance cost**: heavy-write tables pay for every extra index.

sections.title: When this choice makes sense
sections.content: Avoid indexing when the cost outweighs the benefit: **low-cardinality** columns (few distinct values like boolean/gender), **small tables** (a scan is already fast), **write-heavy** columns (each write must update the index), and columns you **rarely filter on**. Every index slows writes and uses space.

When does a SQL query NOT use an index even if one exists?

seo.metaTitle: Database Indexes — What They Are and Why They Matter — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is a database index and why is it important? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Picture the index at the back of a book. A database index works the same way for your table.
speakable_v2.standard_example: a users table looked up by email in a web app

beats.text: A database index is a sorted structure the database keeps next to your table. It's usually a B-tree. It maps a column's values to the rows that hold them. So the database can jump to a row by value, instead of reading the whole table.

Without an index, finding a row by a column means a full table scan. The database reads every single row. On a million-row table that's painfully slow. An index turns that scan into a quick B-tree walk. Reads stay fast as the table grows.

items: Reads get faster. Lookups on WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY use the index instead of scanning.
Writes get slower. Every insert, update, or delete has to update the index too.
It costs storage. Each index is extra data the database stores and maintains.

beats.text: Say users has a million rows. You add CREATE INDEX on the email column. Now a lookup by email drops from a million row reads to about twenty B-tree steps. Here's the non-obvious part. The index helps reads, but it slows every write.

items: Indexing everything. Each extra index slows writes and eats storage, so index only what you filter or join on.
Indexing a low-cardinality column. An index on a boolean barely narrows anything, so the database often skips it.

speakable_v2.cap: So index the columns you actually filter or join on. You trade slower writes for much faster reads.
followup_handoff: How does an index affect INSERT and UPDATE performance?
How do you check if a query is using an index?

questions.question: When should you NOT create an index on a column?
questions.title: When Not to Create an Index in SQL
questions.direct_answer: Do not add an index merely because a column appears in a query. Indexes consume storage and add work to inserts, deletes, and updates. Small tables, rarely used predicates, duplicate indexes, and workloads that must read most rows often favor a scan. Low cardinality alone does not make an index useless: a rare value, partial index, bitmap-style index, or combined key can still be valuable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know indexes have costs and aren't always beneficial.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Indexing every column 'just in case', degrading write performance.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain cardinality and selectivity — indexes help only when they narrow results well.

sections.title: When an Index May Cost More Than It Helps
sections.content:
Indexes can overlap. An index on (customer_id, created_at) may make a separate customer_id index redundant for some workloads, though included columns, sort direction, constraints, and database rules matter.

Before removing an index, check whether it enforces a constraint and whether rare scheduled queries need it. Before adding one, record the slow query and compare execution plans under realistic data. Index design is workload design, not a checklist of forbidden column types.

**Example.** An index on a two-value boolean column in a small table may cost space and extra writes while the optimizer still scans the table. A selective customer_id index on a large orders table can be useful for point lookups; confirm both with query plans.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Evaluate complete queries and selectivity, not a column in isolation.
Every maintained index adds write, storage, cache, and maintenance cost.
A boolean predicate can be useful when one value is rare or a partial index captures it.
Use workload statistics and query plans before adding or dropping an index.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An index on active may be unhelpful when 99% of rows are active and the query returns them all. The same column can be useful for WHERE active = false when failures are 0.1%, especially through a partial index supported by the database. A composite index beginning with tenant_id may also make a low-cardinality status useful inside each tenant. The optimizer cares about estimated cost, not the label 'boolean'.

For example, indexing every column on a write-heavy audit table slows INSERT operations and consumes storage. I add an index for a real query pattern, then check selectivity, write cost, and the execution plan.

sections.title: When NOT to Index
sections.content:
rose|Low cardinality|~few distinct values|boolean, gender|index barely narrows|optimizer skips it
blue|Small tables|~scan already fast|index adds overhead|no real gain|
amber|Write-heavy|~maintenance cost|each write updates index|throttles INSERT/UPDATE|
emerald|Rarely filtered|~no read benefit|but still costs writes|drop unused indexes|

sections.title: A low-selectivity index that won't help
sections.content:
```sql
-- gender has 2 values -> low cardinality, poor selectivity
CREATE INDEX idx_gender ON users(gender);
SELECT * FROM users WHERE gender = 'M';   -- still returns ~half the table
-- the optimizer often ignores this index and scans anyway

-- a high-selectivity index that DOES help:
CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email);   -- email is unique -> narrows to 1 row
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'a@x.com';
```

*High selectivity (unique-ish) helps; low selectivity (few values) usually doesn't.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Indexing 'just in case'**: unused indexes only add write cost and storage.
- **Indexing low-cardinality columns**: booleans/flags rarely benefit.
- **Too many indexes on hot-write tables**: each write updates them all.
- **Never dropping stale indexes**: audit and remove ones no query uses.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A **clustered index** determines the **physical order** of rows on disk — the table *is* the index, so there's only **one** per table (usually the primary key). A **non-clustered index** is a **separate** structure with pointers back to the rows, so you can have **many**.

seo.metaTitle: When Not to Create an Index in SQL — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for When should you NOT create an index on a column? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Not every column deserves an index. Some indexes just cost you writes and storage while helping nothing.
speakable_v2.standard_example: a boolean or status column with only a few distinct values

beats.text: An index is a trade-off, not a default. It speeds up reads, but it slows writes and uses storage. So you only add one when the read win is worth that cost. On some columns, there's no real win at all.

Indexes feel free, but they aren't. Every write has to keep them in sync, and they sit on disk forever. Adding one that no query needs is pure cost. That's why picking the right columns matters more than adding more.

items: Low-cardinality columns. A boolean or a status with two values barely narrows the rows, so the index hardly helps.
Small tables. A quick scan of a few hundred rows beats the overhead of an index lookup.
Write-heavy columns. Every insert and update pays to maintain the index, so heavy writes suffer.
Rarely-filtered columns. If no query filters on it, the index only adds cost.

beats.text: Take a gender column with two values. You index it and run a query for one value. It still returns about half the table. Here's the non-obvious part. The optimizer often ignores that index and scans anyway, because the index saves almost nothing.

items: Indexing just in case. An unused index only adds write cost and storage.
Never dropping stale indexes. Audit them and remove the ones no query uses.

speakable_v2.cap: So index high-cardinality columns you query a lot. Skip small tables, booleans, and fields nobody filters on.
followup_handoff: What is cardinality in the context of indexes?
What is the performance impact of too many indexes on a write-heavy table?

questions.question: What is a composite index and how does column order matter?
questions.title: Composite Index in SQL — Column Order Matters
questions.direct_answer: A composite index stores an ordered key made from several columns. For a typical B-tree index on (a, b), predicates beginning with a are the clearest use of its ordered search range; a query on b alone usually cannot use that leading-key range efficiently. It may still use the index through a scan, skip-scan feature, covering benefit, or database-specific optimization, so 'not usable for b alone' is too absolute.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the leftmost-prefix rule for composite indexes.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting an index on (a, b) to help a query filtering only on b.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Order columns by equality-first then range, and by most-used-in-WHERE leftmost.

sections.title: Composite Index Order and the Leading Columns
sections.content:
Composite design also considers covering columns, sort direction, uniqueness, and range boundaries. With WHERE tenant_id = ? AND created_at >= ?, the equality on the first key selects a tenant and the second key supplies a range. Adding status after that range may help covering but may not further narrow the seek in the same way.

EXPLAIN with production-like data is the final check. An index definition alone does not prove which access path the optimizer will choose.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Match leading columns to common equality/range predicates and ordering needs.
Equality columns before a range often preserve more usable key order.
A b-only query may scan the index or use vendor features, but often needs its own index for efficient lookup.
Check the actual plan and workload; column order is not chosen by selectivity alone.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An index on (tenant_id, created_at) efficiently finds one tenant's newest rows and can support ORDER BY created_at within that tenant. A global created_at query lacks the leading tenant_id predicate, so the engine may scan much more of the index or choose another plan. If that query is important, a separate created_at index may be justified. Some engines have skip-scan behavior, which is why the portable explanation says usually rather than never.

For example, an index on (customer_id, created_at) can support WHERE customer_id=? and a date range for that customer. It usually cannot support a created_at-only lookup as effectively because the leading customer_id is missing.

sections.title: Composite Index at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~multiple columns|in a fixed order|sorted left to right|like a phone book
emerald|Leftmost-prefix|~usable prefixes|(a) yes|(a,b) yes|(b) alone NO
amber|Order rule|~equality then range|=, then >/BETWEEN|most-filtered leftmost|put selective col first
rose|Mistake|~wrong order|index on (a,b)|query on b only|scans instead

sections.title: Leftmost-prefix in action
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_name ON people(last_name, first_name);

SELECT * FROM people WHERE last_name = 'Rao';                       -- uses index (prefix a)
SELECT * FROM people WHERE last_name = 'Rao' AND first_name = 'A';  -- uses index (a, b)
SELECT * FROM people WHERE first_name = 'A';                        -- does NOT use index (b alone)
```

*The index is sorted by `last_name` first, so a `first_name`-only filter can't use it.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting `(b)`-only queries to use an `(a, b)` index**: they can't — leftmost prefix only.
- **Wrong column order**: put the column used in equality/most queries first.
- **Range column too early**: a range (`>`, `BETWEEN`) on a leading column stops the index from using later columns.
- **Duplicate single-column indexes**: an `(a, b)` index already covers `(a)` — a separate `(a)` index is redundant.

followup_questions: How do you order columns in a composite index?
Does an (a, b) index help a query filtering only on b?

seo.metaTitle: Composite Index in SQL — Column Order Matters — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is a composite index and how does column order matter? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Think of a phone book sorted by last name, then first name. A composite index works exactly like that.
speakable_v2.standard_example: an index on last_name then first_name in a people table

beats.text: A typical composite B-tree is ordered lexicographically: first by the leading column, then by the next column within equal leading values. That is why column order affects which lookups and orderings it supports.
Column order gives us the leftmost-prefix rule. The index can serve a query only if it filters from the leftmost column inward. Get the order wrong and the index sits unused, even though it exists.

items: An index on last name then first name helps a filter on last name alone.
It also helps a filter on last name and first name together.
It can't help a filter on first name alone, because the data isn't sorted by first name first.

beats.text: Put the equality column before the range column. Say you filter on status equals active and date after January. Index on status then date works great. Here's the non-obvious part. Once the index hits a range, it can't use the columns after it.

items: Expecting a filter on the second column alone to use the index. Leftmost prefix only.
Adding a separate index on the first column. The composite index already covers it.

speakable_v2.cap: So order the columns to match your most common filter. Put equality columns first, ranges last.
followup_handoff: What is the leftmost prefix rule for composite indexes?
Can a composite index help with an ORDER BY clause?

questions.question: How do you use EXPLAIN to check if a SQL query uses an index?
questions.title: EXPLAIN in SQL — Checking Index Usage
questions.direct_answer: EXPLAIN asks the database to show its planned operators, access paths, join methods, row estimates, and costs. EXPLAIN ANALYZE (name varies) also executes the statement and reports actual timing/rows, so use it carefully for writes and production workloads. An index scan is not automatically good and a table scan is not automatically bad.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know EXPLAIN reveals the plan and how to spot index vs full scan.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Guessing at performance instead of reading the actual execution plan.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the tell-tale outputs (type=ALL, Seq Scan, rows examined) and use EXPLAIN ANALYZE for real timings.

sections.title: Reading an Execution Plan with EXPLAIN
sections.content: Low-cardinality columns are not a universal ban on indexes: bitmap, partial/filtered, covering, or composite indexes can still help specific products and queries. Conversely, a highly selective index can be ignored if a function/cast changes the expression, types do not match, statistics are stale, or another path is cheaper.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Compare estimated rows with actual rows when execution statistics are available.
Look for access path, filters, join order/method, sorting, and repeated loops.
Check the plan with realistic values because selectivity can change the best choice.
Treat product-specific costs as relative planner units, not milliseconds.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=42 may show an index scan on orders(customer_id). If that customer owns most rows, a table scan may be cheaper. EXPLAIN ANALYZE can reveal that the planner estimated 10 rows but read 100,000, pointing to statistics or data-skew work rather than a missing-index assumption.

sections.title: Reading EXPLAIN at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~the execution plan|how the query runs|join order + access type|index or scan?
rose|Full scan signs|~slow on big tables|MySQL type=ALL|Postgres Seq Scan|high rows examined
emerald|Index used signs|~good|MySQL ref/range/const|Postgres Index Scan|fewer rows
amber|EXPLAIN ANALYZE|~real run|actual timings|actual row counts|confirms estimates

sections.title: EXPLAIN before and after an index
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Guessing instead of measuring**: always confirm with EXPLAIN, not intuition.
- **Ignoring `rows` examined**: a high number signals a scan even if an index 'exists'.
- **Function on the column**: `WHERE LOWER(email)=...` shows a scan — the index is bypassed.
- **Trusting estimates only**: use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` for real execution numbers.

sections.title: When this choice makes sense
sections.content: Avoid indexing when the cost outweighs the benefit: **low-cardinality** columns (few distinct values like boolean/gender), **small tables** (a scan is already fast), **write-heavy** columns (each write must update the index), and columns you **rarely filter on**. Every index slows writes and uses space.

followup_questions: What is a database index and why is it important?
What is a composite index and how does column order matter?
When does a SQL query NOT use an index even if one exists?

questions.question: What is the difference between a clustered and non-clustered index?
questions.title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered Index in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A clustered organization stores table rows in or according to one index key, while a secondary/nonclustered index is a separate access structure that points to rows or to the clustered key. A table can have only one physical clustering order, but terminology and behavior vary: InnoDB clusters by the primary key, SQL Server lets one clustered index be chosen, and PostgreSQL's CLUSTER is not automatically maintained as a permanent clustered index.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know a clustered index orders the actual rows while non-clustered is a separate lookup.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking a table can have multiple clustered indexes, or that all indexes are the same.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the extra lookup (bookmark/key lookup) non-clustered indexes need to fetch full rows.

sections.title: Clustered and Secondary Indexes Are Vendor-specific
sections.content:
Clustering can improve range reads when nearby key values correspond to nearby rows, but a wide or random clustering key can increase storage and page splits. Secondary indexes trade additional write and cache cost for alternate access paths.

A correct interview answer should name the database. Without that context, explain the general physical distinction and immediately state that implementation, maintenance, and terminology are engine-specific.

**Example.** In SQL Server, a clustered index organizes the table's data rows by its key, so only one can define that organization; nonclustered indexes contain keys and row locators. PostgreSQL and InnoDB use different storage terms and behavior, so this comparison is product-specific.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: One table can have one current physical row organization but many secondary indexes.
The primary key is not universally the clustered index.
Secondary leaf entries may store row locators or the clustered key depending on the engine.
Use the target database's terminology before applying sizing or lookup rules.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: In SQL Server, a table can be a heap or have one clustered index, which need not be the primary key. In MySQL InnoDB, the primary key is the clustered key and secondary indexes carry that key to locate rows. PostgreSQL can physically reorder a table with CLUSTER, but later writes are not kept in strict clustering order. Therefore 'the table is the index and it is usually the primary key' describes some engines, not SQL in general.

sections.title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered
sections.content:
blue|Clustered|~orders the rows|table IS the index|one per table|usually the PK
emerald|Non-clustered|~separate structure|holds key + pointer|many per table|points to the row
amber|Lookup|~extra step|non-clustered -> key lookup|to fetch other columns|covering index avoids it
rose|Trade-off|~range vs point|clustered great for ranges|non-clustered great for point lookups|

sections.title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered
sections.content:
| Aspect | Clustered | Non-Clustered |
|---|---|---|
| Stores | the actual rows (ordered) | key + pointer to row |
| Per table | exactly one | many |
| Physical order | yes (defines it) | no |
| Typical | primary key | secondary lookups |
| Extra lookup | no | yes (to fetch full row) |

sections.title: One physical order — the clustered index
Many separate structures — non-clustered indexes
sections.content:
```sql
-- a non-clustered index: separate B-tree with a pointer back to the row
CREATE INDEX idx_customer ON orders(customer_id);

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7;
-- finds matching keys in idx_customer, then does a key lookup
-- into the clustered index to fetch total, etc.
```

*Clustered = the table sorted itself; non-clustered = a side index pointing into it.*

sections.title: When to Use Which
sections.content:
The **clustered index** is usually the **primary key** and is great for range queries (rows are physically contiguous). Choose it on a column you scan by ranges or join on most.

Add **non-clustered indexes** on other columns you frequently filter or join on (e.g., `email`, `customer_id`). Make them **covering** (include the selected columns) to avoid the extra key lookup on hot queries.

followup_questions: Why can a table have only one clustered index?
What is a key lookup or bookmark lookup?

seo.metaTitle: Clustered vs Non-Clustered Index in SQL — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer

speakable_v2.standard_example: an orders table with a primary key and a non-clustered index on customer_id

beats.text: A clustered index sets the physical order of the rows on disk. The table itself lives in that order, so there's only one per table. A non-clustered index is a separate structure. It holds the key plus a pointer back to the row, and many can exist per table.

values: None, the row is right there.
Often one, to fetch other columns.

beats.text: The clustered index is usually the primary key. It's great for range scans, because the rows sit next to each other on disk. Reach for non-clustered indexes on other columns you filter or join on. Good picks are email or customer id.
Look up an order by customer id with a non-clustered index. It finds the key, then jumps to the clustered index for the rest. The gotcha's the extra hop, and that's why people add covering indexes.

speakable_v2.cap: So the clustered index is the table's own order. Everything else is a side index pointing back in.

questions.question: When does a SQL query NOT use an index even if one exists?
questions.title: Cases Where SQL Index is Not Used
questions.direct_answer: An optimizer can skip an index when a scan is estimated cheaper or when a predicate cannot form a useful search range. Common causes include returning much of the table, mismatched leading columns, non-sargable expressions, implicit conversions, stale estimates, and a leading wildcard in an ordinary B-tree text search. These are tendencies, not universal prohibitions; expression indexes and database-specific access methods can support some cases.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know why a query skips an existing index (non-sargable predicates, selectivity).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping the indexed column in a function and wondering why the index isn't used.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Define 'sargable' and rewrite YEAR(d)=2026 as a date range.

sections.title: Why an Optimizer May Skip an Existing Index
sections.content:
Sargable means the engine can use an indexed search argument effectively. Rewriting YEAR(created_at) = 2026 as a half-open range often helps because it preserves the raw column, but a matching expression index is another option.

Index hints should be a last resort because data distributions and engine versions change. Fix type mismatches and statistics, design suitable indexes, and let measured plans guide the decision.

**Example.** WHERE LOWER(email)=? may not use a plain index on email unless the database can transform it or has a matching expression index. WHERE name LIKE '%son' also cannot use a normal leading B-tree search in the usual way; specialized indexes may help.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: A function on a column may need a matching expression/function-based index.
LIKE '%term' usually cannot use a normal leading-key B-tree seek, but trigram/full-text indexes may help.
A scan can be the correct plan for many matching rows or a small table.
Compare estimates and actual rows with the database's plan tools.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
WHERE LOWER(email) = ? may miss a plain email B-tree seek, while an index on LOWER(email) can support it in databases with expression indexes. WHERE created_at >= ? can use an index, yet the optimizer may choose a table scan when almost every row matches. That is not an error. Rewriting every predicate to 'force the index' can make performance worse.

For example, a query returning most rows may correctly choose a table scan, while LOWER(email)=? may need a matching expression index. I check the actual plan instead of assuming an index must be used.

sections.title: Why Indexes Get Skipped
sections.content:
rose|Function on column|~non-sargable|YEAR(d)=2026|LOWER(email)=...|index bypassed
blue|Leading wildcard|~LIKE '%x'|B-tree unusable|prefix LIKE 'x%' is fine|
amber|Type cast|~implicit conversion|string vs number|cast hides the column|match types
emerald|Low selectivity|~optimizer choice|matches many rows|scan judged cheaper|index not worth it

sections.title: Non-sargable: function hides the column
sections.content:
```sql
-- index on created is IGNORED because YEAR() wraps the column
CREATE INDEX idx_created ON orders(created);
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE YEAR(created) = 2026;   -- full scan
```

sections.title: Sargable: keep the column bare, use a range
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created >= '2026-01-01' AND created < '2027-01-01';  -- uses idx_created
```

*Same result, but the column is untouched on the left, so the B-tree index applies.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wrapping the column in a function**: breaks index usage — rewrite as a range.
- **Leading wildcard `LIKE '%x'`**: forces a scan — use full-text search.
- **Type mismatches**: compare same types to avoid implicit casts.
- **Assuming an index is always used**: the optimizer may choose a scan for low selectivity.

sections.title: When this choice makes sense
sections.content: Avoid indexing when the cost outweighs the benefit: **low-cardinality** columns (few distinct values like boolean/gender), **small tables** (a scan is already fast), **write-heavy** columns (each write must update the index), and columns you **rarely filter on**. Every index slows writes and uses space.

seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for When does a SQL query NOT use an index even if one exists? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: The index exists, but the database still won't use it. One small slip in your WHERE clause hides it.
speakable_v2.standard_example: WHERE YEAR(created) = 2026 skipping an index on the created column

beats.text: A query can skip an index even when one exists. The usual cause is a predicate the index can't match. We call a matchable predicate sargable. Break sargability and the database falls back to a full scan.

This trips people up because the query still works. It returns the right rows, just slowly. Nothing errors out, so the slow scan hides in plain sight. Knowing the common causes saves you hours of confusion.

items: A function on the column. Wrapping the column in YEAR hides the raw value, so the index is skipped.
A leading wildcard. LIKE with a percent at the start gives the B-tree no prefix to follow.
A type mismatch. Comparing a number column to a string forces a cast that bypasses the index.
Low selectivity. If the filter matches most rows, the optimizer picks a scan on purpose.

beats.text: You filter with WHERE YEAR of created equals 2026. The index on created goes unused. Rewrite it as created on or after January first and before next January. Here's the non-obvious part. Same rows, but now the column stays bare, so the index works.

items: Wrapping the column in a function and expecting the index to work. Rewrite it as a range instead.
Trusting that an index always gets used. The optimizer decides, so confirm with EXPLAIN.

speakable_v2.cap: So keep predicates sargable. Leave the column bare, match types, and lean on ranges over functions.
